title: Sloppy start to NFL season 'super frustrating' for Tony Dungy | Exclusive
description: Tony Dungy was connected to the NFL for 46 years as a player, coach and broadcaster. He has a different view this season.
fullText:
Tony Dungy is watching the NFL with a different purpose these days – there's no game plan to execute or strategy to analyze for millions of viewers on live TV – and the Hall of Fame coach is not so thrilled.

The first two weeks of the NFL season have left Dungy bemoaning sloppy football that reminds him of the preseason.

"Super frustrating to me," Dungy told USA TODAY Sports this week. "I think people are doing a disservice to their team by not playing players in the preseason, not getting them ready. I've seen guys who looked like they were not ready for the speed of the game because they didn't play in the preseason.

"I don't think it will be until October when we can say who's good and who isn't because I think a lot of these teams are still getting ready to play."

Dungy said that as a coach, he can understand the rationale behind not playing starters – and particularly quarterbacks – during preseason. It's the injury risk. Except for the teams that play in the Hall of Fame Game, teams play just three preseason games. And about half the teams didn't put their starting quarterback on the field in preseason.

When Dungy coached (through the 2008 season), teams played four preseason games and his starters typically played about six quarters across the contests. Starters – including his franchise quarterback – would go for about three quarters in the third preseason game, then sit out the preseason finale.

"I cannot imagine, if I told Peyton Manning, 'Hey, you're not going to play at all, the first snap of the regular season is going to be your first live snap,' I don't think he would have been very happy about that," Dungy said. "Now, a lot of people are doing it."

That's not all that Dungy, 70, is getting used to. This is the first time in 46 years that he hasn't been connected to the NFL as a player, coach or broadcaster. The past 17 years he served as an analyst for "Football Night in America," part of the "Sunday Night Football" package on NBC, but Dungy and former all-pro safety Rodney Harrison were not renewed as part of a revamped show that now includes former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin.

"They felt it was time," Dungy said. "Whether they wanted to be younger, whether they wanted to have different voices, I don't know. Rodney and I were there 17 years. We had a lot of fun together and I made some great friendships. It was special to me because I got to maintain a lot of relationships and see people and talk to guys and kind of stay in the game without being in it 24/7.

"I just look at now like God's got another plan and something else, and it'll be a different phase. But it was a neat 17 years."

Coincidentally, Dungy also wasn't retained after six years as a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Selection committee. The size of the committee was reduced from 50 voters to 25 (plus three alternates) as part of sweeping changes.

"I'm not bitter or upset or anything about not being on," Dungy said. "They asked for my time on the committee, I did it, I enjoyed it. It wasn't easy, but it was something I felt good about doing."

Dungy, a devout Christian who lives in Tampa, is eager to continue walking the walk of a faith that he has publicly professed throughout his career – and sometimes drawn criticism for. Given his numerous charity efforts, spiritual outreach and potential media projects, there won't be much of a void, if any, on his calendar without his national TV job.

On Saturday, Dungy will conduct the chapel service for the Minnesota Vikings after their arrival in town. He also spoke to the football team at Central Florida and this week conducted a Zoom chat with Wake Forest's baseball team.

"In the past, I'd have to say I couldn't do it in the fall because I'm occupied," he said.

Dungy is also brainstorming with James Brown, the host of CBS' "NFL Today" and his longtime friend, about developing a faith-based podcast. And he's taped about 10 interviews with players and coaches for a project being shopped, dubbed "Road to Sunday," that will delve into backstories essential to their journeys.

"All of them talked about the Lord without being asked. It was crazy!" Dungy said of the interviews. "To be able to talk about what guys are doing off the field, what's on their heart, what's inspired them and how they got there, who was key in their lives, I think we can tell some positive sports stories that the world needs."

In the meantime, Dungy will still see the NFL through the eyes of a coach, analyst and player.

"I saw the Bucs play on TV and they had four fumbles," he said, referring to the Week 1 loss at Cincinnati. "It just looked like guys are not ready for contact. And I saw a lot of blown coverages, people going in motion and getting wide open. I saw a lot of tackling that looked like what you'd do at practice – where you hit the guys but you don't wrap them up. You let them keep running and you don't take people to the ground. It looked like the same thing.

"I know they are going to be better, they are going to be sharper, and it's a long season. But these first two weeks, I've seen a lot of up and down play that you don't expect."

At this point, Dungy says that offenses – with timing sharpened by 7-on-7 non-contract drills – have a distinct advantage over defenses.

"In the old days, it used to be the opposite," he said.

Interestingly, Dungy said that he and Tomlin – who was hired by Dungy an a NFL coach and now replaces him on the NBC set – talked about how defenses are hard-pressed to keep up because CBA rules limit contact in practices.

Of course, it's no surprise that Dungy – a college quarterback who converted to safety in the NFL and former defensive coordinator – has a nerve struck for defense.

"The way the practice schedules are set up, with what you can and can't do, it's harder on defense," Dungy said. "It's hard to get that physicalness, the reaction time and everything.

"I look at Denver and Houston as two of the best defenses last year and they both had most of their guys back. And they're giving up 30 points in a game (in Week 1). You're saying, 'Wait a minute. Are these the same guys?' They are, but they're not playing the same way. So I think some of these teams are going to be what they were and some may not."

Either way, it will be a different type of must-see TV for Dungy.

title: Explained: Why Cricket West Indies slashed player salaries by 25%, suspended Super50, & what it means for 2027 World Cup
description: Why did Cricket West Indies slash player retainers by 25% and suspend the Super50? We explain the Caribbean cash crisis and its impact on the 2027 World Cup.
fullText:
Explained: Why Cricket West Indies slashed player salaries by 25%, suspended Super50, & what it means for 2027 World Cup originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Cricket West Indies has slashed international retainer fees by 25 per cent while shifting domestic players onto shorter seven-month contracts.

The board has suspended this year's men's Super50 and women's T20 Blaze tournaments, citing unsustainable operational and travel costs across the region.

CWI is redirecting its focus and resources toward preparing the men's ODI squad for the crucial 2027 World Cup qualifier campaign.

Cricket West Indies has pulled the trigger on an overhaul of its finances and domestic structure, and has rolled out a package of cost-cutting measures the board says is meant to tackle a deepening financial, developmental and competitive crunch.

International players will keep their 12-month contracts, but the money attached to them is shrinking by 25 per cent. Domestic cricketers face an even bigger structural shift, moving from full-year deals down to seven-month retainer contracts instead. Given how many West Indies players already lean toward franchise leagues over central contracts, this cut risks accelerating that trend rather than slowing it down.

CWI chief executive Chris Dehring is framing the pay cut as a reluctant but necessary call. However, before getting into the specifics, he acknowledged the players' side had cooperated through a difficult process.

"International retainer contracts will remain at 12 months but there will be a 25% reduction on the retainer fees," he said.

"We appreciate the spirit of cooperation of the West Indies Players Association and the players who have demonstrated their total understanding of the circumstances we all face. While not ideal, it is a necessary step towards financial stability."

MORE: 'Time to measure up': Daren Sammy issues rallying cry ahead of IND vs WI ODIs to end West Indies' 24-year series drought

CWI confirmed that this year's men's Super50 and women's T20 Blaze tournaments won't go ahead, and pointed to the sheer cost of running domestic competitions across a region spread over multiple independent nations.

That's a significant blow to the traditional route into the men's ODI team, especially with West Indies staring down a World Cup qualifier in February-March 2027 after already missing the 2023 edition of the tournament.

MORE: Rohit, Virat back in action: Gill-led India to assemble in Thiruvananthapuram for WI ODIs

Dehring didn't mince words when explaining just how unsustainable the current model had become, walking through the financial reality before laying out the raw numbers.

"Our domestic tournaments as structured historically, where Cricket West Indies bears the entire cost of every national team and tournament - whether it is age-group, development or senior for both men and women - including salaries, match fees, airfares, hotels and event staging costs, are simply unsustainable," he said.

"The high cost of domestic travel and accommodation absorbs too much of our scarce resources every year instead of being deployed for the direct benefit of our cricket."

He then pointed to a massive figure that's been quietly draining the board's coffers for over a decade, which shows just how one-sided the arrangement with domestic airlines has been:

"Indeed, over eighty million US dollars has been spent by Cricket West Indies with domestic airlines over the past 15 years, without receiving a dollar of sponsorship from those beneficiaries," he added.

"We must also deal with the immediate cash crunch brought about by years of bearing this burden and the crippling financial losses that emanate as a result."

MORE: Shamar Joseph gestures to Kieron Pollard to 'shut up' in apparent disrespect before wild celebration to WI legend's dismissal

With the domestic calendar trimmed back, CWI will now focus on preparing the men's ODI squad for 2027 ODI Qualifiers.

A string of white-ball fixtures against a touring England A side in November will lead into a dedicated ODI team camp, which will give the squad the best possible pathway to get ready for February's qualifiers.

However, amid the cash crunch, the ICC had sanctioned a loan to the board, but the terms and conditions are proving to be a hindrance.

"In July of this year the ICC approved a loan facility to Cricket West Indies totaling US$16 million to provide temporary relief to our chronic cashflow challenge, available in 3 tranches over the next year," the statement said.

"As with any other lender, this loan comes with terms of repayment and conditions that will require Cricket West Indies to attain critical metrics in order to access those funds starting this month."

MORE: 'Next Andre Russell': Former RCB analyst introduces WI cricket's next Dre Russ

This restructuring lands at an awkward moment too, with West Indies cricket's unusual multi-nation setup now facing fresh demands ahead of the 2027 Pan American Games in Lima and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The top four sides from the 2025-26 Super50 and T20 Blaze editions have already locked in their Pan American Games spots, but with those tournaments now suspended, CWI has unveiled replacement invitational events for Olympic qualification instead.

Dehring laid out how this new invitational structure is meant to work, framing it as a chance for individual nations to take ownership of their Olympic ambitions.

"These replacement tournaments will be by invitation to the 10 countries under the aegis of Cricket West Indies that qualify for Olympic participation," he said.

"We are excited by these new invitational tournaments...It's an opportunity for individual countries to galvanize national resources to chase Olympic glory, with the responsibility and cost of participation falling on their respective national cricket and Olympic associations, private sectors, governments and people. The winners of those tournaments will qualify for the ICC Olympic Qualifying tournaments for a spot in Los Angeles in 2028."

There's no sugar-coating this: an $80 million airline bill over 15 years with nothing coming back in sponsorship is the kind of number that demands drastic action, and Dehring deserves some credit for laying the figures out instead of burying them.

But the timing couldn't be worse. Cutting pay just as franchise leagues keep poaching West Indies talent risks pushing more players away from the international setup altogether, right when the team needs its best players available for a qualifier campaign that could decide whether they even make the 2027 World Cup.

Moreover, suspending Super50 also guts the one domestic tournament that's actually produced proven ODI performers in recent years. The decision to push the financial burden of Olympic qualification onto individual boards might work in theory, but smaller nations within the West Indies structure simply don't have the private-sector or government backing to make that work evenly. This is survival mode, not a growth strategy, and West Indies cricket can't afford many more rounds of it.

fullText:
Sports Director Ralf Kellermann says: "Ann-Sophie is one of the longest-serving players at BVB, and with her mentality, dedication, and physicality, she has not only become a key pillar of the team but also a great role model. That's why we're very happy to have set the course early on to continue down this successful path together with her."

Vogel joined BVB from VfL Bochum in 2024. In her first season, she immediately won the triple—the Westphalian Championship, the District Cup, and the Westphalian Cup—with Borussia Dortmund. With 63 competitive appearances for the Black and Yellows, she holds the record for most appearances on the current roster. She has scored eight goals and provided 28 assists so far—also the current team high.

"Something truly great is taking shape here, and it fills me with pride and joy that I get to help shape this journey. I'm delighted that the coaching staff and club officials have placed their trust in me and see something in me that can continue to benefit the club and the team in the future," said Ann-Sophie Vogel.

title: North Providence football stays unbeaten with second straight shutout
description: Here's how North Providence football grabbed its second shutout victory of the year.
fullText:
NORTH PROVIDENCE — North Providence football knows its formula.

Two sacks on the opening drive, a special teams edge and a touchdown on the first offensive possession. Another three shutout quarters of North Providence football followed for a third straight win.

It's all about business in North Providence and the Cougars are loving it. Running back Kaiden Wray supplied two touchdowns in a 12-0 victory over Middletown on a cool Thursday night in North Providence. It's the second consecutive shutout for the Cougars after silencing Rogers, 6-0, last week. The 3-0 start began with a thumping of Pilgrim in Week 1.

"North Providence, we play gritty football," linebacker Quentin Forkpa said. "A win is a win, defensive shutout. That's what we pride ourselves in. Hard defense and hard offense. Our offensive line guys are always pushing. They set the tone in practice, always working hard."

Wray took North Providence's first offensive snap off the right side for a 10-yard touchdown. A pair of tackles for losses by Grant Washington and Dominick Moise pushed the Islanders back into their own end. And a low snap on the ensuing punt put the hosts in prime scoring position to start Thursday night.

The senior's second touchdown — the catch of a 12-yard pass by Gian Renzi — was scored with 49 seconds left in the half. North Providence held Middletown scoreless after the Islanders had a first-and-10 at the Cougars' 11. North Providence, on the ensuing possession, punted out of its own end but recovered a loose ball in the sequence. Renzi then finished off the nearly six-minute drive with a swing pass to Wray to double the lead.

"When the defense is playing lights out and we're getting that push up front and we're getting the stops in the backfield, it makes a huge impact on the game," Renzi said. "Being able to go out, perform on both sides of the ball, and then special teams. Week 1, we had our struggles with special teams and defense, but we came back 100 percent in practice and you can see the difference."

North Providence held Middletown to just one possession in the second half. It halted the Islanders again in the red zone, after a first-and-goal from the 6, to seal the shutout. The Cougars kept possession for the final 7:59 to send Middletown away. It's not the flashiest brand of football like the tempo offenses that have taken over. But it works and the Cougars aren't going to stop.

"I can't always be content with where I'm at," Wray said. "We always want to get better, so it's just great to come out here. Shutout last week, it was great to come back. Shutout again and put up more points."

There's a belief in North Providence that makes everything work. They were decked out in their yellow alternate jerseys with blue and white trim — a welcomed surprise to the team last year. And they have one of the better pregame walkouts in the state as the Cougars descend onto the field from the school.

Those things matter when building a culture. North Providence isn't far removed from winning its Division IV title in 2023. It captured four wins in Division III last year and has nearly matched that mark already with this formula.

"When [the jerseys] got brought out, it definitely gave us a little extra push to go out there and get the job done," Renzi said. "Look good, play good. We get to go out and put these uniforms on and put out for our school. It feels great."

Sorgi, who the Badgers were able to flip from Louisville, has family ties to the program as his father, Jim, played at UW from 2000-03.

Knowing his father has NFL experience with the Indianapolis Colts and New York Giants, it comes as no surprise that Sorgi is having this much success during his senior season.

title: Predictions: Michigan State football vs. Nebraska
description: Angelique S. Chengelis, Connor Earegood, John Niyo, and Bob Wojnowski of The Detroit News predict the outcome of Saturday's MSU-Nebraska game.
fullText:
Angelique S. Chengelis, Connor Earegood, John Niyo, and Bob Wojnowski of The Detroit News predict the outcome of Saturday's Michigan State-Nebraska game at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing (5 p.m., Big Ten Network/760).

▶ Angelique S. Chengelis: The Spartans fought hard at Notre Dame in a loss last weekend and had to feel encouraged by their performance heading into the Big Ten schedule. Nebraska is unbeaten and the Cornhuskers' statistics suggest a balanced team, the defense ranked 11th nationally and the offense 10th. They've held teams to an average 11.7 points, which ranks 16th nationally in scoring defense, but they did not face an overly challenging non-conference schedule. Still, quarterback Anthony Colandrea has been solid, but the key, not surprisingly, will be which team wins in the trenches. Pick: Nebraska, 24-20

▶ Connor Earegood: Nothing about Nebraska's schedule tells you anything about the kind of team it is. A loss at Notre Dame at least showed you that Michigan State can hang around with a tough opponent. The Spartans left South Bend banged up and bruised, but also encouraged as much as they could be by a close loss. This defense, led by Jordan Hall, doesn't give up easily, though its corners need to take a step — especially with a test against Cornhuskers' phenom Jacory Barney Jr. Offensively, Michigan State doesn't have the talent upside to play one-dimensional when its ground game gets bottled. MSU is 26-19 in Big Ten play the past 10 years when it wins its opener. It's 9-34 when it loses it. Pick: Michigan State, 23-13

More: Big Ten opener against Nebraska vital to starting Spartans off right

▶ John Niyo: Nebraska hasn't played a Power Four team yet, so it's hard to know what to make of their 3-0 start. There's ample reason to be skeptical, too, given Matt Rhule's track record since arriving in Lincoln. But the Huskers' offense does look different with a confident, mobile quarterback in Anthony Colandrea and a deeper, more talented line blocking for him. Pat Fitzgerald's first Big Ten game is another important measuring stick in Year 1, but I wonder about the injury toll that trip to South Bend took on the Spartans. Pick: Nebraska, 28-24

▶ Bob Wojnowski: The Cornhuskers average 46 points and 520 yards per game, but proper context is required. They beat North Dakota, Bowling Green and Ohio at home. But they do have an experienced, efficient quarterback in senior Anthony Colandrea and an outstanding freshman running back in Jamal Rule. Michigan State's defense held up decently against Notre Dame, thanks to a monstrous game from Jordan Hall. If his ailing arm cooperates, Hall could be a game-changer here. The Spartans didn't run well against the Irish, and Alessio Milivojevic spent the second half running for his life. The offensive line remains a work in progress, but Pat Fitzgerald loves his team's fight. That's important, because this looks like a typical Big Ten slugfest. Pick: Nebraska, 24-17

title: Royals 'not starstruck' by PSG visit for AI summit
description: Reading Head of AI Stuart Fenton says Paris Saint-Germain's visit for a technology summit shows the progress the Royals have made.
fullText:
Reading Head of AI Stuart Fenton says Paris St-Germain's visit to the League One club for a summit on the technology shows the progress the Royals have made.

The reigning European champions and Dutch giants Ajax are among the clubs participating in the conference at Reading's Bearwood Park training complex on Friday, a year after the Royals set up a pioneering AI department driven by new owner Rob Couhig.

"PSG won the Champions League last year, so it's super exciting that we get teams like that coming to Reading," Fenton told BBC Radio Berkshire.

"We're doing some really good things here but it's not in isolation. We want to hear what some of these top teams around the world are doing.

"It also puts Reading in the conversation with those kinds of people. Every football fan - I'm a Reading fan myself - dreams of those European nights playing these teams.

"We're having the conversation with them around AI in football and where football's going.

"That's a real testament to the programme we're running here and how much advancement we've made in the last year."

Reading need to tidy up results on the road - Roberts

Inspired by the success teams such as Brighton & Hove Albion and Brentford have had through their use of data, Reading are using AI predominantly for recruitment but have also applied it to areas including tactics, retail and tending to the turf at their Select Car Leasing Stadium home.

"It's [about] creating the culture across the club where people are thinking differently - not how we can use it to replace humans, but how we can empower them and actually get them to do their job in a more effective way," said Fenton, who is the first Head of AI in English football.

"We've got some really talented people here but one of the big challenges is that data is huge in football.

"How do we use the AI and technology available to effectively streamline that data and give our team more information on players all across the world?

"Everyone thinks AI is like a light switch - you flick it and suddenly you're the world's most intelligent team. If it was that easy, everybody would be doing it. The benefits for us compound across the club.

"I had our ground staff come to me yesterday saying they're now using AI when they're doing the grass cutting. The models are looking at grass protection. AI is giving them the best possible formulas [in terms of] what they need.

"It's impacting everything across the club. What really excites me is when somebody comes up to me and says 'Stu - I've had this idea. Can we do it?'

"We've already started putting certain things in place. It's creating that culture of innovation across a football team."

Premier League side Crystal Palace and Champions League club Como are among the visitors who will hear about Reading's work and share their insights, with the event also being used to launch a new programme between the club and Setanta College on sports technology and artificial intelligence.

"We're not starstruck by these teams," added Fenton. "The exciting thing is they're coming to us - we're not going to them."

Arsenal forward Havertz was subbed off in the first half of Thursday's 1-1 draw with the Netherlands in Amsterdam with what appeared to be a hamstring injury.

In a statement, the DFB said he suffered a "muscle strain" but did not indicate how long the 27-year-old was likely to be out of action.

Bayern Muninch's Musiala, 23, was injured in the warm-up on Thursday and took no part in the match.

The DFB said a scan showed a muscle tear in his thigh.

Having initially named two squads as part of a 44-man group for the four international matches, Germany coach Jurgen Klopp has brought in forwards Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt from the second set-up to replace the duo for Sunday's match against Greece in Augsburg.

title: ‘It’s crazy for teams to deal with that’: Frustrating presidential policy sparks reactions before Donald Trump appearance
description: United States President Donald Trump is set to attend Saturday afternoon’s showdown between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns in Knoxville. fullText:
United States President Donald Trump is set to attend Saturday afternoon's showdown between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns in Knoxville. It's widely known that the president's attendance at any public event causes a lot of logistical challenges, but it's safe to say that not many people knew about how Trump's appearance could directly impact the game itself.

As the Longhorns prepare for the road showdown with Tennessee, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian gave some rather unique insight into one of the challenges that come along with Trump attending games, and the sports media world was stunned by his revelations.

During his Thursday press conference, Sarkisian revealed that this actually is not the first time that he will be involved in a game that Trump has attended. Sarkisian was the offensive coordinator at Alabama under Nick Saban when Trump attended the College Football Playoff National Championship following the 2017 season.

Given this experience, Sarkisian has some unique insight that he was able to share.

Sarkisian revealed that whenever the president moves throughout the stadium, all communication throughout the stadium has to be shut down, including the communication between the coordinators in the booth and the sideline as well as the in-helmet comms for the players.

"One thing we have to be aware of is when the President goes to a game, any time he enters, leaves or changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication," Sarkisian said during his Thursday Zoom press availability, via 247Sports. "They cut all communication, so they cut your headsets to coaches and they cut headsets with coach-to-player communication."

Sarkisian added that this can happen without any warning, even for something simple like the president using the restroom.

"So, you have to have a plan for that, if and or when it happens and you don't get any warning," Sarkisian said. "It just cuts out. So, you have to have a plan for that and adjust. If he comes in the middle of the first quarter and leaves in the fourth quarter or if he decides use the restroom, whatever it is, you have to be prepared for that."

Sarkisian went on to reveal that the Miami Hurricanes and the Indiana Hoosiers actually had to deal with these issues during the national championship game.

Needless to say, Sarkisian's revelation seemingly caught the sports world off guard, as several high-profile sports commentators, analysts, and personalities had no idea that this was even an issue.

"Have to admit, didn't know this one…" wrote former ESPN star Gene Wojciechowski.

"I did not realize football helmet communication gets shut off if the president gets up to go to the bathroom," wrote Chris Vianni of The Athletic.

"So if the president decides to go pee during an important 3rd down or a late offensive possession the comms go out and they have to signal in the plays? Seems like a big deal," wrote Geoff Schwartz of Fox Sports.

"I get why that's in place, but it's CRAZY for teams to deal with that. Wonder how the Lions/Commanders navigated that last year," wrote Detroit Lions beat writer Jeremy Reisman of Pride of Detroit.

"That's actually kind of wild," wrote NFL insider Albert Breer.

"It's gotta be like using your phone on the NYC subway with this president's bladder," joked broadcaster and journalist Master Tesfatsion of Bleacher Report and Amazon Prime Video.

It's certainly a unique challenge. We'll have to see whether or not it comes into play on Saturday.

title: Atalanta’s Charles De Ketelaere reveals PSG talks
description: Atalanta forward Charles De Ketelaere (25) has revealed that he held talks with Paris Saint-Germain this summer, before the reigning European champions ultimately set their sights on Spain’s Ferran ...
fullText:
Atalanta forward Charles De Ketelaere (25) has revealed that he held talks with Paris Saint-Germain this summer, before the reigning European champions ultimately set their sights on Spain's Ferran Torres (26).

PSG refreshed their attack this summer. Out went Bradley Barcola, Randal Kolo Muani, Lee Kang-in, and Goncalo Ramos, and in came Mika Godts, Maghnes Akliouche, and Torres. The latter has started in spectacular form, scoring seven goals since making the move from Barcelona. However, things could have been different.

De Ketelaere, speaking in an interview with La Dernière Heure, has revealed that he joined PSG instead of Torres. "There were clubs interested, but when you see the prices being paid in the current market, it isn't always easy to leave," said the former AC Milan forward. "I know that Atalanta were asking for a lot, I think it was around €50m."

That fee is what Les Parisiens paid to sign Torres, just weeks after he netted the winner for Spain in the FIFA World Cup final. "You have to find a team that will pay it," De Ketelaere continued. "In the Premier League, there are several teams that can do it, but it didn't happen. I spoke with PSG but they ultimately chose Ferran Torres. I am happy at Atalanta. I know how important it is to be a starter following my adventure at AC Milan."

At PSG, De Ketelaere likely would have been a rotation option and perhaps sparsely used in the big UEFA Champions League fixtures, although Torres' strong start saw him also start their UCL opener against Slovan Bratislava, during which he netted a hat-trick.

title: Theranos founder reportedly to be transferred to halfway home next year
description: Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2022 but has seen her sentenced reduced several times
fullText:
Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2022 but has seen her sentenced reduced several times

Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos, will reportedly be transferred from a minimum security prison to a halfway home next August.

In 2022, Holmes, 42, was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison for defrauding Theranos investors out of hundreds of millions of dollars and ordered to pay restitution. The company falsely promoted its technology as being capable of detecting diseases, including types of cancer, from drops of finger-pricked blood.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) informed Holmes’s victims of the upcoming move to the Austin transitional center in Del Valle, Texas, according to ABC News. The New York Times and NBC News confirmed ABC’s reporting.

While Holmes has been incarcerated at the federal prison center in Bryan, Texas, her prison term has been reduced several times.

The US district judge Edward Davila wrote in court filings that her shortened sentence did not diminish the weight of her fraudulent behavior. “Holmes’s revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance,” Davila said, according to ABC News.

She is set to leave prison in February 2030, BOP records show.

ABC News reported that Holmes plans to reside in Austin after her release.

Holmes has faced renewed interest as the subject of comedian Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary You Can See Everything. The enigmatic project follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans before her prison term and through the start of her incarceration.

In May, NPR reported that Evans had raised millions for a new medical testing startup, a revelation that fueled speculation over Holmes’s post-prison plans.

title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
fullText:
How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence
from 41 Countries

 Working Paper

 New technologies can raise demand for some workers while lowering it for others, but knowing which workers gain and which lose is challenging. We study this question for generative AI. Our model decomposes changes in labor demand following firm AI adoption into a firm-wide productivity effect and worker-type-specific changes in task content. We take the model to the data, analyzing a sample of 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records across 41 countries.

 We infer AI adoption from job advertisements that involve generative AI use. An instrumented event study shows that foreign affiliates of AI-adopting companies reduce the junior share of their workforce relative to comparable control affiliates. The decline primarily comes from growth in senior employment rather than from a fall in junior employment, with suggestive evidence of modest overall employment growth. Senior employment shifts toward AI-exposed occupations, while our point estimates suggest a shift away from these occupations among juniors. The model-based decomposition provides suggestive evidence of modest productivity gains from AI adoption.

title: 'We didn't need air conditioning': the airport cooled by natural ventilation
description: At Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, the ceiling design funnels a light tropical breeze into the terminal
fullText:
At Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, the ceiling design funnels a light tropical breeze into the terminal

At the arrivals terminal at Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, visitors are greeted by floor-to-ceiling windows framing the lush green mountains of the French Indian Ocean territory.

What they may have also expected was the icy chill of air conditioning; this island just off Madagascar sits in the tropical zone to the south of the equator. But instead, the terminal is cooled by a light tropical breeze, the result of natural ventilation built into its unique design.

The genesis of the project was in 2016, as part of a wider effort by airport management to reduce its carbon dioxide emissions. Marc Delanoë, who was then leading the airport’s environmental and energy team, was determined from the beginning that the new arrivals terminal, which was being built completely from scratch, would not use air conditioning.

“I took on the responsibility to prove to my management that not using air conditioning was feasible,” said Delanoë, now the airport’s sustainable development director. “So, from the start, we never thought of this building having air conditioning being an option. It was a risky bet, but the further we went with our studies, the more we realised that we were right.”

The roof of the terminal, which opened in 2024, curves upwards from each of the rectangular building’s long sides in gentle waves. But, instead of meeting in the middle, the roofs end abruptly to form a “canyon”. The creation of an area of low pressure funnels wind into the building through vents on each side that are adjusted depending on the weather conditions.

Ceiling fans with a 7.5-metre (24.6ft) diameter help to circulate the air. In the 30C (86F) humid heat of Réunion’s wet summers, which last from around November to April, the resulting breeze reduces the perceived temperature by four to five degrees, to almost the same level usually set for air conditioning.

Less air is allowed to flow in during the island’s dry winters, when the coastal daytime temperature falls to 25C and below. During a cyclone, the entire building is closed up.

The building’s lead architect, AIA Life Designers, said it wanted to challenge the assumption that adjusting temperature was the only way for humans to cope with heat.

“It is precisely this pitfall – understanding summer comfort solely through the lens of indoor temperature – that we want to dismantle, a pitfall that traps us in the logic of air conditioning as the only answer to comfort requirements,” said Éric Bussolino, the firm’s engineering and environment director.

“Our objective is to maintain an indoor air temperature identical to the outdoor temperature while generating an airflow of 1 metre per second to reduce the perceived temperature for passengers.”

AIA, chosen for its expertise in designing airport buildings, partnered with a local architect, Olivier Brabant, who had the necessary expertise of designing buildings for the island’s tropical maritime climate, Delanoë said.

Local architects were already using natural ventilation on the island, in everything from offices and libraries to a university amphitheatre designed by Brabant. “We simply had to change the scale,” Delanoë said.

“You have to channel the air, play with the elements … That’s exactly what our ancestors did on La Réunion,” he said. “They built houses according to the direction of the wind, with a central corridor, and they opened the windows or closed the doors depending on the amount of air that they wanted to let in. If they were cold, they closed them; if they were hot, they opened them.”

Building the arrivals terminal cost €75m , of which €15m went on a new baggage sorting system and €60m on the building, said Delanoë. Since opening two years ago, the airport has saved €150,000 a year in energy bills, he said. AIA said this amounted to savings of about 60% compared with an air-conditioned building, while carbon emissions were lower by a factor of eight.

Delphine Robert, who leads the local tourism board’s welcome team, works in the terminal once a week and said she preferred it to other offices.

“It’s very airy. It’s comfortable – a lot of light, the ventilation is optimal,” she said. “I find it better working in this building, because I am often sick. And that’s the result of air conditioning, which is very strong in offices. So that’s why it’s more pleasant to work in a building where the air circulates, but it is natural.”

The lessons from the terminal’s natural ventilation will be harder to apply in large, polluted cities in mainland Europe, said Delanoë. “You will concentrate the pollutants inside – it doesn’t work,” he said. “We are lucky, we are on an island, there is no pollution around.”

Continental Europe, which is struggling to adapt to heatwaves being made ever more severe by the climate crisis, would also have to eschew air conditioning to make use of natural ventilation, Delanoë said.

“The problem is that if you have air conditioning at home and you have air conditioning in your car, when you get to the office, if you don’t have air conditioning, you’re going to be hot, he said.

“That is to say that if you reduce air conditioning throughout your life … when you get to 30 degrees in the office, you won’t be hot. In La Réunion, people are used to 30 degrees.”

title: Instrumental Monitor Evasion Emerges Under Ordinary Task Pressure
description: A central concern in AI safety is that agents may treat oversight as an obstacle when it conflicts with completing their goals. We study instrumental evasion, the propensity of LLM agents to circumvent runtime monitoring as a means of completing ordinary tasks. We introduce EvasionBench, a benchmark of 50 diverse task-policy pairs in which completing the task requires an operation prohibited by a runtime monitor. Agents know that their tool calls are monitored and are prompted to continue working when they pause. Across our evaluations, best-of-3 evasion attempt rates reach up to 98% and success rates up to 88%, with substantial variance across models.

title: Agentic CUDA Kernel Optimizer
description: A langgraph based workflow with a C++ CUDA suite to optimize CUDA kernels - bertaye/agentic-cuda-optimizer
fullText:
An agentic CUDA kernel optimizer that turns workload descriptions into GPU implementations through an automated cycle of code generation, correctness checks, benchmarking, and refinement. Powered by LangGraph, the agent explores kernel implementations and launch configurations, queries GPU properties, and can research NVIDIA documentation for optimization guidance and inspect Nsight Compute counters to inform its next experiment. Each experiment is recorded, and the fastest validated implementation is retained.

The model can change both kernel code and per-case launch configurations. A standalone C++ harness compiles kernels with NVRTC, launches them through the CUDA Driver API, and saves outputs. Python handles comparison and candidate selection.

Every case must pass validation. Ranking uses the geometric mean of latency across performance cases; small correctness cases do not affect the score. Timing defaults to 10 warmup launches and 100 measured launches using CUDA events. Compilation time and profiler replay timings are excluded from ranking.

Developed on Windows with an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU. Requires Python 3.12+, an NVIDIA GPU and compatible CUDA Toolkit/driver, CMake 3.24+, a C++17 compiler, and an OpenAI API key. The build commands below use Visual Studio 2026 with the C++ tools installed.

Create a .env file in the repository root:

The default model is gpt-5-mini with medium reasoning effort. API usage is billed to your account. Use -h for all options, or --config optimizer_agent/example.json for the included configuration example.

Supply your own workload components with --signature, --reference, --initial-kernel, and --input-cases. Omitted components are inferred or generated. To continue from an earlier run using its saved inputs:

This example assumes the earlier run generated reference.cu; supplied references are saved as supplied-reference.cu. Input manifests retain paths to their binary data, so keep those files available.

Float32 GEMM on an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, with NVIDIA research and Nsight Compute enabled.

Each session gets a directory under results/run-NNN/ containing kernel sources, requests, input/output data, model/tool responses, history.json, and summary.json. Successful runs export best.cu, per-case replay requests, and heatmap.png/heatmap.svg. Nsight reports are saved when profiling is enabled.

This is an experimental optimizer for individual kernels. Passing supplied cases does not prove general correctness, and a generated reference is not an independent correctness oracle. Improvements are workload-dependent; no comparison against cuBLAS or other vendor libraries is currently included. Keep the GPU otherwise idle when comparing timings.

Generated input scripts execute locally as Python subprocesses without a sandbox. Generated CUDA kernels also run on the local GPU.

The graph below is rendered from the compiled LangGraph workflow with Nsight profiling enabled. Dashed edges are conditional routes. Without --use-nsight, evaluation routes directly to the next attempt or finalization; NVIDIA research is skipped unless --nvidia-research is set.

fullText:
A federal appeals court has rebuffed a Trump administration effort to dictate how homeless service organizations in Los Angeles can seek millions of dollars in funding from the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The ruling released Thursday also frees up federal funding that already had been approved but not distributed to homeless service organizations in Los Angeles.

At issue was whether the Los Angles Homeless Services Authority could submit an application on behalf of dozens of organizations seeking $239 million in federal funds.

In a 2-1 decision posted Thursday, the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a district court ruling that restored LAHSA as the applicant for the organizations seeking federal funds.

HUD suspended LAHSA in June, citing a record of mismanagement, and said organizations should apply directly to the government for the 2026-27 funding cycle. The initial application deadline was the end of August.

LAHSA sued to block the move. District Court Judge David O. Carter issued a preliminary injunction finding that HUD acted arbitrarily and capriciously and ordered it to restore LAHSA's authority. He set a trial date in February.

HUD then appealed, seeking a stay.

In its bluntly worded decision, the appellate panel denied the department's request, finding that HUD "chose to suspend LAHSA at a time when it would leave the Los Angeles region particularly vulnerable" with ill effects on "vulnerable populations, critical programs and ongoing services."

"It is likely that its plan is unworkable and, at this late stage, extremely difficult if not virtually impossible to implement," the decision said.

Stephanie Graves, chair of the LAHSA Commission, applauded the court's ruling. "For the thousands of people experiencing homelessness or working to rebuild their lives, the systems and funding that connect them to housing and services cannot simply stop," Graves said in a statement. "Today's decision allows that work to continue while the larger issues are resolved."

The new deadline to apply for HUD funding is Oct. 14, and LAHSA's Interim Chief Executive Officer Gita O'Neill said the agency is "moving at full speed" to meet that deadline.

In addition to leaving LAHSA as the applicant for this funding cycle, the order also requires HUD to release funds from last year's grants that had been approved but not formally released by the department, forcing about a dozen Los Angeles organizations to operate for months without reimbursement.

"Today's 9th Circuit decision is welcome news for the survivors of domestic violence and their children who depend on Jewish Family Service LA's Hope Transitional Shelter," the group said in a statement. "But a court ruling alone does not solve our funding crisis."

Since April 1, the shelter has operated without $300,000 in promised government funding, covering half its budget.

"HUD's appeal is still underway, and until these funds actually reach providers, the situation at our Hope Transitional Shelter remains critical," the statement said.

The order also restored LAHSA's other core functions — operating the homeless database and the housing matching system and conducting the annual homeless count. But the reprieve is only temporary. As directed in Carter's ruling, the board of the federally mandated committee that has perennially selected LAHSA for those functions issued a request for proposals from other applicants.

Los Angeles County, which last year diverted its more than $300 million in homeless funds from LAHSA to the new Department of Homeless Services and Housing, applied to take over all those functions.

Thursday's decision was signed by justices Jacqueline H. Nguyen, an Obama appointee and Roopali H. Desai, a Biden appointee. Trump appointee Ryan D. Nelso dissented.

James Copenhaver was one of three attendees struck by gunfire.

One of the spectators shot during the assassination attempt on then-presidential candidate Donald Trump during a 2024 campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died, officials and his family attorney said Thursday.

James Copenhaver, 76, of Moon Township, died on Wednesday "surrounded by his loved ones," an attorney for his family said in a statement.

Copenhaver was one of three attendees struck when a gunman opened fire at the rally in Butler on July 13, 2024, according to Pennsylvania State Police.

He was "gravely wounded" in the shooting, attorney Joseph Feldman said in a statement on behalf of Copenhaver's family.

"Throughout that difficult time, James faced every challenge with the same strength and resolve that defined his life, and the kindness shown by so many brought great comfort to him and to those who love him," Feldman said.

Copenhaver and his family "have been deeply grateful for the outpouring of love, prayers, and support they have received over the past two years," Feldman said.

Copenhaver is remembered by his family as a "devoted husband, father, and grandfather" and a veteran of the armed forces whose "dedication to this great country was a defining part of his life," Feldman said.

Copenhaver died at a hospital in Pittsburgh on Wednesday, according to the Allegheny County Office of the Medical Examiner. The cause and manner of death are pending, it told ABC News on Thursday.

Trump called Copenhaver a "true American Patriot" in a statement on social media Thursday, saying his death is a "tremendous loss."

"His indelible legacy of love and devotion will forever endure," Trump said.

House Republicans addressed Copenhaver's death in a statement Thursday, saying he "endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

"We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time. May he rest in peace," the statement said.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also extended his condolences to Copenhaver's family.

"The political violence that occurred in Butler, Pennsylvania on July 13, 2024 is never okay," Shapiro said in a statement Thursday. "I said it at the time in Butler and I say it again today: we all have a responsibility to take down the temperature, rise above hateful rhetoric, and search for a brighter future for this nation."

Former Marine David Dutch was also injured in the assassination attempt, police said. He was shot in the chest and liver and was initially in a medically induced coma after the shooting, according to the Marine Corps League of Pennsylvania.

The third attendee struck by gunfire -- 50-year-old firefighter Corey Comperatore -- died shielding his family, officials said.

Trump was grazed in the ear by a bullet.

Officials said the gunman -- 20-year-old Thomas Matthew Crooks of Bethel Park, Pennsylvania -- fired up to eight shots from the roof of a nearby building before a Secret Service sharpshooter shot and killed him.

fullText:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Residents along Mexico's west coast stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes, while Hawaii's Big Island and Maui braced for potentially catastrophic flooding, as separate hurricanes swirled in the Pacific on Thursday.

Nolo became a hurricane in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday night and was expected to strengthen while turning toward the Big Island, the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters warned that the Big Island could see rainfall totals of 15 to 30 inches (38 to 76 centimeters), with higher amounts possible through Saturday. The island of Maui also could be hit with life-threatening floods, the hurricane center said.

Meanwhile, heavy rains from powerful Hurricane Polo could cause torrential flooding and landslides in Mexico, according to the U.S. hurricane center. In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas, seawater already swept through homes Thursday and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets.

Polo has fluctuated between Category 4 and 5, both major-hurricane strength. It was expected to regain Category 5 status on Friday, then gradually weaken Friday night and Saturday, the hurricane center said.

After skirting Mexico's coast, Polo was expected to move farther out to sea Thursday night and Friday before hooking back toward land to the north on Saturday.

The series of powerful storms comes as the weather phenomenon El Niño prompts major environmental shifts across the world, fueling drought in some areas and flooding in others. El Niño traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.

Hawaii has been battered this year by major flooding in the spring, an earthquake and two other hurricanes since mid-August.

"In my 20 years of experience here, I've never seen three hurricane watches for the islands in the same year," said John Bravender of the National Weather Service in Honolulu.

Mexican authorities were opening shelters and clearing people from beaches, while coastal residents tried to protect businesses from getting swept away. People in high-risk areas were being evacuated, though authorities didn't immediately say how many.

Much of the worry from locals comes from hurricanes in past years that devastated cities along the Pacific coast. Hurricane Otis in 2023 unexpectedly plunged Acapulco into turmoil for weeks.

"So many people said it wouldn't happen and then it did. After that, you're left on edge," said Gonzalo Ramírez, a bartender in the city.

Polo posed the biggest threat to Guerrero and Michoacán, neighboring states in southwest Mexico that share a long coastline scattered with small ports, tourist towns and fishing villages. Much of the area is marked by poverty, and residents routinely complain they are left to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Mexican authorities have deployed 15,000 security personnel across the coast and suspended schools.

In Lázaro Cárdenas, a port city in Michoacán that was hit with high surf, locals and government officials were clearing out piles of wooden planks from a number of destroyed ramadas and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 15-foot (4.5-meter) waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damaged house, Contreras worried how she would economically recover.

"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

While the Big Island is expected to bear the brunt of Nolo, its full path remains uncertain, according to Bravender, the weather service's warning coordination meteorologist in Hawaii.

Most concerning, he said Thursday, is that the heaviest rain is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation.

"There are several communities that were isolated, flooded, roads that were washed out," he said. "It's that same area that is most under threat," Bravender said.

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed for the rest of the week.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month's Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the coming storm.

A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was centered far from land, roughly 1,110 miles (1,785 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula.

In the northern Atlantic Ocean, Tropical Storm Fay re-formed early Thursday, the U.S. hurricane center said. It was nearly 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) west-southwest of the Azores.

Tropical Storm Gonzalo formed in the Atlantic Ocean late Thursday, about 190 miles (306 kilometers) southeast of the Cape Verde islands off the coast of West Africa. The U.S. hurricane center said that if it stays on its current track, the storm will pass near or over portions of the islands Friday.

Aoun Angueira reported from San Diego. Associated Press journalists John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and Jeriel Vargas Ambriz in Lázaro Cárdena, Mexico, contributed to this report.

title: Iran's president says Tehran wants a deal with U.S. before the midterms
description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressing the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday. (Selcuk Acar / Anadolu via Getty Images)
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S.
fullText:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” Pezeshkian added, referring to a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. The agreement, signed in June, eventually collapsed.

In response to NBC News’ request for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said: “The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region.”

“The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable,” Kelly added.

Pezeshkian’s comments came two days after President Donald Trump said in a speech to world leaders at the U.N. that he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the fall elections.

“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November contests. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a group of reporters in a separate briefing in New York on Thursday that a plan has been presented to U.S. officials through mediators during talks this week that would lead to the opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of talks after seven days.

Araghchi said the plan could begin as soon as the U.S. agreed to it and maintained that the plan did not go beyond the agreement signed by Trump in June, commonly referred to as a memorandum of understanding.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that, if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days and talks will be restarted,” Araghchi said. “The conditions we have asked the U.S. to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the U.S. president.”

Araghchi pointed out that one of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump on Tuesday also defended the conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country or make a deal.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.

In the exchange with news organizations, Pezeshkian said he has met with the Islamic Republic’s new leader twice — including a month ago, for seven hours.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei assumed the role in early March after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an Israeli attack that also killed family members and other senior leaders.

Pezeshkian said he did not see “any issues with his health or physical appearance” in their meetings, adding that they sat on the floor on traditional pillows. Mojtaba Khamenei was severely injured in the strike that killed his father, three people with knowledge of the matter told NBC News in July, with burns to his face and body and wounds that have required several operations to one of his legs.

Iran’s president briefly addressed other pressing issues affecting the relationship between Tehran and Washington. He said his government was “open” to inspections of its nuclear facilities, which the regime has long maintained are for civilian purposes, and he insisted the regime was not seeking to assassinate the American president.

“This has not been the position of the Iranian government that we seek to assassinate President Trump or his family members,” Pezeshkian said.

The Justice Department charged an Iranian man in November in an alleged murder-for-hire effort to kill Trump when he was the Republican presidential candidate in 2024.

Two others were charged with planning to kill an Iranian American journalist and activist who has criticized the Iranian government over its treatment of women.

U.S. authorities said the plot was part of Iran’s efforts to avenge the death of a top Iranian general, Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in Baghdad in a U.S. drone strike Trump ordered during his first term in the White House.

Pezeshkian has previously denied an Iranian plot to kill Trump, telling NBC News’ Lester Holt in Tehran last year that the regime would “never” do so.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A tech-heavy guest list, the fashion choices of those on it, who sat where and what was on the menu marked the softer — often and glitzier — details of diplomacy as Donald Trump threw a Thursday night state dinner honoring China's leader Xi Jinping.

The event featured a cavalcade of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that most excite Trump, who has a reputation for reveling in hosting parties.

"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Trump has done his best to impress Xi during China's leader's during Xi's three-day visit to Washington, and praised their close personal relationship — even as he has decried top Democratic candidates as "communists" ahead of the November midterm elections.

Xi and Trump discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours — even as an ongoing First Amendment fight over press access at the White House has unfolded. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, including letting him tour his Marine One presidential helicopter and a new helipad he built for it — before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal.

Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."

"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.

Trump wore a tuxedo, and her office said first lady Melania Trump opted for a tuxedo-style outfit: a white Saint Laurent cotton poplin blouse, a black silk cummerbund and black brocade pants — both from Dolce & Gabbana — with a peony motif.

Xi chose a black suit and his wife, Peng Liyuan, wore a red gown. The East Room, where the dinner was held, featured low lighting and place settings with elegant red and gold decor.

Those in attendance included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who signed autographs upon arriving at the White House. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opted for a tuxedo over his trademark black leather jacket. Bernard Arnault, the CEO of French luxury goods company LVMH, walked through black security fencing to enter the event.

The president toasted his strong relationship with Xi and the bond between the U.S. and China, but then added, "If I could go off script just for a second, I just want to say I had to do it," as those assembled laughed.

"I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back," Trump said, referring to the construction site of his White House ballroom on the South Lawn, which he said, "you've heard so much about."

Trump said the project was a year from completion, and said he thought attendees "will see something that I think you will really love."

The president said that after the dinner attendees could go see the worksite and be "the first people to step foot" on it.

"We'll do that. Maybe after we've finished with the entertainment tonight," Trump said, asking, "Anybody wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and sparkling, it's our honor to have you do so."

Trump has called the ballroom he's building the "Great Hall of the United States," and suggested it could rival the Great Hall of the People, where he dined during a state visit to Beijing in May.

The president also presented Xi with an eagle statue that he said was designed "in personal collaboration with Melania and myself." Xi did not present Trump a public gift in return during the dinner.

The first lady helped craft the evening's menu, which was served on the red china from Ronald Reagan's presidency. It featured a first course of yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, fresh herbs, crispy pancetta and drizzled scallion oil.

After that, guests got sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte. Dessert was vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House.

The dinner came after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their state visit guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.

Thursday's dinner was packed with technology industry titans like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman, and Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell.

During his own visit to Beijing in May, Xi hosted Trump for a state dinner that unfolded beneath grand chandeliers in the Great Hall of the People. That event also included many tech luminaries, such as Tim Cook, formerly Apple's CEO, and Musk.

It was all a stark departure from 2015, when then-President Barack Obama was preparing to host Xi for a state visit and Trump — in the midst of his first presidential run — criticized all the hubbub.

"Just take them to McDonald's and go back to the negotiating table," Trump said then, during a rally in South Carolina. He later conceded on Fox News Channel that Xi might at least be worthy of getting "probably a double-size Big Mac."

title: Mortgage rates top 7% as an already tough housing market gets tougher
description:
An aerial view of a housing development on August 08, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. - Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
Mortgage rates reached a grim milestone this week, topping 7% for the first time since January 2025 and reaching their highest level during either of Donald Trump’s presidential terms.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 7.03% this week, up from 6.95% last week, according to data released Thursday by Freddie Mac.
fullText:
Mortgage rates reached a grim milestone this week, topping 7% for the first time since January 2025 and reaching their highest level during either of Donald Trump’s presidential terms.

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 7.03% this week, up from 6.95% last week, according to data released Thursday by Freddie Mac.

It’s the fifth-straight week of rising mortgage rates, putting a deeper squeeze on housing affordability. Higher rates mean larger monthly payments and less purchasing power for buyers.

“Beyond the immediate financial constraints, the 7% threshold is a foreboding psychological barrier,” said Bright MLS chief economist Lisa Sturtevant. “Crossing this mark could create a chilling effect on the market, leading to home sales transactions to slow considerably this fall.”

However, mortgage rates remain well below the 7.79% peak they hit in 2023, when inflation was running at decades-high levels.

About seven months ago, the average 30-year mortgage rate briefly dipped below 6% for the first time in years, prompting hopes that cheaper borrowing would finally unfreeze the housing market. Instead, those hopes have faded as the war in Iran has pushed oil prices higher, adding fresh pressure to overall inflation and mortgage rates.

Consider the difference between a homebuyer who locked in their mortgage rate in February, when the average briefly fell to 5.98%, and someone buying today. On a median-priced home with a 20% down payment, today’s buyer would pay hundreds of thousands of dollars 

“Expect 7% as the new normal,” said Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, in a blog post last week.

Action in the bond market is the chief cause for higher mortgage rates. US bond yields have climbed this year, pushing up interest rates across the economy.

The 10-year US Treasury yield is a benchmark for mortgage rates: They loosely track the 10-year, which moves with investors’ expectations for rate decisions by the Federal Reserve, but also inflation and growth expectations.

As the 10-year yield has climbed this year, mortgage rates have pushed higher. And this week, the 10-year Treasury yield surged to its highest level in nearly two decades after fresh data on Wednesday pointed to a strong economy and intensifying inflation nerves.

The 10-year yield started the year at around 4.15%, and is now trading around 5.15%, its highest level since 2007. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.16% at the start of the year.

Bond yields are rising as markets adjust to central banks starting to raise interest rates to tamp down inflation driven in large part by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.

The move higher in bond yields raises the cost of borrowing money, and some economists worry that yields have reached levels that could pose a risk for the broader economy.

Higher bond yields translate into higher mortgage rates, as well as auto loans, consumer loans and commercial loans.

When Trump left office in January 2021, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate was just below 2.8%.

A property developer and real estate investor himself, Trump placed the blame for the subsequent rise in mortgage rates squarely on the Fed’s shoulders. While mortgage rates don’t directly follow the central bank’s policy moves, Trump often berated former Fed Chair Jerome Powell for failing to lower the Fed’s benchmark interest rate quickly enough when inflation initially spiked during the early years of the pandemic.

Last week, Trump’s handpicked successor to Powell, Kevin Warsh, announced that the central bank hiked interest rates by a quarter point – its first hike since July 2023 – in an attempt to tamp down inflation. The central bank’s members have indicated they foresee at least one other rate hike in 2026.

On his social media platform Truth Social, Trump posted last week that “interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less,” a significant drop from the Fed’s current rate range of 3.75% to 4%.

Higher rates are already starting to slow down the housing market.

Shares of some of the country’s largest homebuilders, including Lennar (LEN), D.R. Horton (DHI) and PulteGroup (PHM), have fallen over the past month as higher borrowing costs threaten to weigh on both home sales and new construction.

Last week, Lennar CEO Stuart Miller warned that many homebuyers are “clearly stretching” to afford to afford a home lately, attributing the company’s disappointing earnings to higher mortgage rates and stubborn inflation.

Although the pace of home sales have remained largely unchanged this year compared to last year, according to NAR data through August, there are some signs that higher mortgage rates have started scaring off some buyers.

Pending home sales, which measure the number of homes under contract, rose 0.3% in August from July, but fell 4.7% from a year ago, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Mortgage applications to buy a new home fell 11% last week from the same week a year ago, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data released on Wednesday.

Among those still looking to buy, more borrowers are turning to adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs – a riskier loan product that played a role in the housing market’s buildup to the 2008 financial crisis.

Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for an ARM last week, according to the MBA. These loans typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can face sharply higher monthly payments.

Rates on 5/1 ARMs – which are fixed for five years and then adjust annually – were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed-rate loans last week, said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s chief economist.

Home prices have yet to reflect a national slowdown in demand, though. The median existing home price was $429,100 in August, the 38th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases, according to NAR.
